method: COMPILED FROM 2 SOURCES. S1: PARAPHRASED AND HASH-ANCHORED from European Dermatology Forum, European Association of Dermato-Oncology and EORTC (Lebbé C, et al.), European Journal of Cancer 2019;114:117–127 'Diagnosis and treatment of Kaposi's sarcoma: European consensus-based interdisciplinary guideline (EDF/EADO/EORTC)' (published June 2019), 24 claims; LICENCE: © 2019 Elsevier Ltd. All rights reserved (free to read; publisher PDF from the University of Szeged repository, publicatio.bibl.u-szeged.hu/21424) (read at copyright line in the retrieved PDF; Unpaywall lists it as free-to-read ('other-oa')). S2: QUOTED from Revenko A, Shirron N, Shainer R, et al. (narrative review), Cancers (Basel) 2026;18(6):1008 (doi 10.3390/cancers18061008) 'Classic Kaposi Sarcoma: Current Treatment Strategies and Emerging Therapeutic Approaches' (published 20 March 2026), 13 claims; LICENCE: CC BY 4.0 (read at Europe PMC fullTextXML <license> element for PMC13024955). Verify each source separately: verify.py --source <file> --only-source S<n>. Edition 2.0 keeps every S1 claim unchanged and adds S2, a CC BY 2026 narrative review of classic Kaposi sarcoma, quoted, for staging, local-therapy response rates, PLD and taxane detail, pomalidomide, immunotherapy and interferon dosing. The file kaposi-sarcoma.layout.txt is a second extraction of S1 (same guideline), not a second source; one Europe PMC search found no newer open KS guideline. S2's Tables 1-2 were stripped in edition 2.0. Table rows appended with pmc_text.py --append-tables (2026-09-24); claims from S2 Table 1 (recommended systemic therapies for classic KS) and Table 2 (ongoing trials) are quoted from the row lines.

claims.claim: **Kaposi sarcoma is a multicentric tumour of lymphatic-endothelial cells infected with HHV-8.** Its four subtypes are classic, endemic (sub-Saharan Africa), epidemic (HIV) and iatrogenic (immunosuppression, especially transplant); the degree of immunosuppression drives onset and progression.
claims.locator: European Dermatology Forum, European Association of Dermato-Oncology and EORTC (Lebbé C, et al.), European Journal of Cancer 2019;114:117–127, 'Diagnosis and treatment of Kaposi's sarcoma: European consensus-based interdisciplinary guideline (EDF/EADO/EORTC)', published June 2019, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ejca.2018.12.036, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Lesions are purple, red-blue or brown macules, plaques or nodules** that can bleed, ulcerate or become warty; lymphoedema is common and may appear first.
claims.locator: European Dermatology Forum, European Association of Dermato-Oncology and EORTC (Lebbé C, et al.), European Journal of Cancer 2019;114:117–127, 'Diagnosis and treatment of Kaposi's sarcoma: European consensus-based interdisciplinary guideline (EDF/EADO/EORTC)', published June 2019, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ejca.2018.12.036, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Classic KS is usually indolent; HIV-related and post-transplant KS can be extensive and life-threatening.**
claims.locator: European Dermatology Forum, European Association of Dermato-Oncology and EORTC (Lebbé C, et al.), European Journal of Cancer 2019;114:117–127, 'Diagnosis and treatment of Kaposi's sarcoma: European consensus-based interdisciplinary guideline (EDF/EADO/EORTC)', published June 2019, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ejca.2018.12.036, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **In HIV, KS remains the second most common cancer in Western countries.** Low CD4 is the main risk factor, but risk stays above the general population even with normal CD4 and suppressed viral load.
claims.locator: European Dermatology Forum, European Association of Dermato-Oncology and EORTC (Lebbé C, et al.), European Journal of Cancer 2019;114:117–127, 'Diagnosis and treatment of Kaposi's sarcoma: European consensus-based interdisciplinary guideline (EDF/EADO/EORTC)', published June 2019, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ejca.2018.12.036, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **After organ transplant, KS risk is 50- to 500-fold higher,** peaking in the first 2 years; median onset is 13 months after transplant.
claims.locator: European Dermatology Forum, European Association of Dermato-Oncology and EORTC (Lebbé C, et al.), European Journal of Cancer 2019;114:117–127, 'Diagnosis and treatment of Kaposi's sarcoma: European consensus-based interdisciplinary guideline (EDF/EADO/EORTC)', published June 2019, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ejca.2018.12.036, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Biopsy is mandatory.** Staining for the HHV-8 LANA protein is the best way to tell KS from its mimics.
claims.locator: European Dermatology Forum, European Association of Dermato-Oncology and EORTC (Lebbé C, et al.), European Journal of Cancer 2019;114:117–127, 'Diagnosis and treatment of Kaposi's sarcoma: European consensus-based interdisciplinary guideline (EDF/EADO/EORTC)', published June 2019, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ejca.2018.12.036, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **HHV-8 viral load in blood is not usable** to monitor KS or predict it in transplant recipients.
claims.locator: European Dermatology Forum, European Association of Dermato-Oncology and EORTC (Lebbé C, et al.), European Journal of Cancer 2019;114:117–127, 'Diagnosis and treatment of Kaposi's sarcoma: European consensus-based interdisciplinary guideline (EDF/EADO/EORTC)', published June 2019, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ejca.2018.12.036, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Only AIDS-related KS has a validated staging system (ACTG: tumour, immune, systemic symptoms);** since antiretroviral therapy, the tumour and symptom components carry the prognosis. Otherwise, sort patients into localised non-aggressive, locally aggressive or disseminated disease.
claims.locator: European Dermatology Forum, European Association of Dermato-Oncology and EORTC (Lebbé C, et al.), European Journal of Cancer 2019;114:117–127, 'Diagnosis and treatment of Kaposi's sarcoma: European consensus-based interdisciplinary guideline (EDF/EADO/EORTC)', published June 2019, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ejca.2018.12.036, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **For classic KS, Brambilla's staging is now preferred over Krigel's:** stage I small macules confined to the lower limbs, II larger plaques still on the lower limbs, III multiple plaques and nodules on the lower limbs, IV lesions beyond the lower limbs.
claims.source_text: Historically, CKS staging was based on Krigel's classification, but more recent reviews suggest that Brambilla's classification provides a more accurate framework []. In this system, stage I (macronodular) includes small macules confined to the lower extremities; stage II (infiltrative) involves larger plaques still limited to the lower extremities; stage III (florid) includes multiple plaques and nodules in the lower extremities; and stage IV (disseminated) includes lesions extending beyond the lower extremities [].
claims.locator: Revenko A, Shirron N, Shainer R, et al. (narrative review), Cancers (Basel) 2026;18(6):1008 (doi 10.3390/cancers18061008), 'Classic Kaposi Sarcoma: Current Treatment Strategies and Emerging Therapeutic Approaches', published 20 March 2026, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13024955/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Work-up for classic KS (NCCN, via S2):** clinical photography at baseline and follow-up and a chest X-ray; CT only for new gut or chest symptoms or unexpected findings. FDG PET/CT finds extracutaneous spread but misses some gut mucosal lesions.
claims.source_text: However, NCCN guidelines recommend clinical photography as an essential component of the initial workup and follow-up. While chest X-ray is indicated to screen for thoracic involvement, CT is reserved for specific clinical scenarios, such as onset of new gastrointestinal or pulmonary symptoms or to investigate abnormalities found during routine monitoring. … Finally, whole body FDG PET\CT is a valuable tool for identifying extracutaneous extensions, but it remains less sensitive in detecting lesions within the mucosal surfaces of the digestive tract [,].
claims.locator: Revenko A, Shirron N, Shainer R, et al. (narrative review), Cancers (Basel) 2026;18(6):1008 (doi 10.3390/cancers18061008), 'Classic Kaposi Sarcoma: Current Treatment Strategies and Emerging Therapeutic Approaches', published 20 March 2026, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13024955/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Because KS is multifocal, treating one lesion does not stop new ones and aggressive sarcoma-style surgery is not indicated.** Watchful observation suits asymptomatic immunocompetent patients; treat symptomatic lesions locally, and use systemic therapy for florid, disseminated or rapidly progressive disease or when local treatment fails.
claims.source_text: Because KS is driven by latent KSHV infection and typically presents as a multifocal disease, treatment of a single lesion does not prevent the development of additional lesions. Therefore, aggressive surgical resection, as used for other soft-tissue sarcomas, is generally not indicated. Watchful observation may be appropriate for immunocompetent patients without symptoms. Symptomatic lesions can be effectively managed with topical therapies, radiotherapy, or surgical excision. In cases of florid or disseminated disease, or in infiltrative stages with rapid progression or resistance to local treatments, systemic therapy is usually the preferred treatment option [,].
claims.locator: Revenko A, Shirron N, Shainer R, et al. (narrative review), Cancers (Basel) 2026;18(6):1008 (doi 10.3390/cancers18061008), 'Classic Kaposi Sarcoma: Current Treatment Strategies and Emerging Therapeutic Approaches', published 20 March 2026, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13024955/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Radiotherapy in classic KS: overall response 88–100%, complete response 58–93%, symptom relief in 95–100%;** randomised data show hypofractionated schedules work as well as conventional ones. Brachytherapy suits small lesions. Side effects (dry desquamation, pigmentation, lymphoedema) often improve.
claims.source_text: KS is a radiosensitive tumor [], and radiotherapy remains a cornerstone in the management of localized CKS, achieving overall response rates of 88-100% [,], with a complete response rate of 58-93% [,], and symptomatic relief in 95-100% of patients [,]. Radiotherapy (RT) has also been shown to be effective for both mucosal and cutaneous lesions []. Several RT regimens can be used for palliation and local disease control, and randomized data suggest that hypo-fractionated regimens are as effective as conventional fractionation []. … Brachytherapy represents an alternative RT modality, demonstrating high response rates in small lesions, especially in elderly patients or in cases where cosmetic outcomes are a concern []. Radiotherapy is generally well tolerated, with adverse effects such as dry desquamation, hyperpigmentation, and lymphedema, which often improve during follow-up [,].
claims.locator: Revenko A, Shirron N, Shainer R, et al. (narrative review), Cancers (Basel) 2026;18(6):1008 (doi 10.3390/cancers18061008), 'Classic Kaposi Sarcoma: Current Treatment Strategies and Emerging Therapeutic Approaches', published 20 March 2026, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13024955/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **No randomised trial compares the local options.**
claims.locator: European Dermatology Forum, European Association of Dermato-Oncology and EORTC (Lebbé C, et al.), European Journal of Cancer 2019;114:117–127, 'Diagnosis and treatment of Kaposi's sarcoma: European consensus-based interdisciplinary guideline (EDF/EADO/EORTC)', published June 2019, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ejca.2018.12.036, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Radiotherapy is among the most effective treatments for localised KS** (response 47% to 99%). Avoid more than 3 Gy per fraction and concurrent systemic therapy to limit late effects.
claims.locator: European Dermatology Forum, European Association of Dermato-Oncology and EORTC (Lebbé C, et al.), European Journal of Cancer 2019;114:117–127, 'Diagnosis and treatment of Kaposi's sarcoma: European consensus-based interdisciplinary guideline (EDF/EADO/EORTC)', published June 2019, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ejca.2018.12.036, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Surgery recurs often;** keep it for a few small, well-defined superficial lesions.
claims.locator: European Dermatology Forum, European Association of Dermato-Oncology and EORTC (Lebbé C, et al.), European Journal of Cancer 2019;114:117–127, 'Diagnosis and treatment of Kaposi's sarcoma: European consensus-based interdisciplinary guideline (EDF/EADO/EORTC)', published June 2019, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ejca.2018.12.036, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **CO2 laser or superficial cryotherapy can work for a while on superficial lesions;** warn about lasting hypopigmentation.
claims.locator: European Dermatology Forum, European Association of Dermato-Oncology and EORTC (Lebbé C, et al.), European Journal of Cancer 2019;114:117–127, 'Diagnosis and treatment of Kaposi's sarcoma: European consensus-based interdisciplinary guideline (EDF/EADO/EORTC)', published June 2019, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ejca.2018.12.036, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Intralesional chemotherapy** (vinblastine, response about 70%) and **electrochemotherapy** (bleomycin with electroporation) are effective local options.
claims.locator: European Dermatology Forum, European Association of Dermato-Oncology and EORTC (Lebbé C, et al.), European Journal of Cancer 2019;114:117–127, 'Diagnosis and treatment of Kaposi's sarcoma: European consensus-based interdisciplinary guideline (EDF/EADO/EORTC)', published June 2019, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ejca.2018.12.036, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Topical options:** imiquimod helped about half of 17 patients with classic or endemic KS (local itch and redness in 53%); alitretinoin 0.1% gel gave a 37% response in HIV-related KS on antiretrovirals.
claims.locator: European Dermatology Forum, European Association of Dermato-Oncology and EORTC (Lebbé C, et al.), European Journal of Cancer 2019;114:117–127, 'Diagnosis and treatment of Kaposi's sarcoma: European consensus-based interdisciplinary guideline (EDF/EADO/EORTC)', published June 2019, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ejca.2018.12.036, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Other local response rates (S2):** imiquimod 5% cream about one-third complete and one-third partial response (47% in an HIV-negative phase I–II study); intralesional vincristine complete response up to 76%; electrochemotherapy with bleomycin complete response 65–89%; liquid-nitrogen cryotherapy complete remission in 63% (19/30).
claims.source_text: Topical imiquimod 5% cream acts as a Toll-like receptor 7 agonist, enhancing local immune activation, inhibiting angiogenesis, and inducing endothelial apoptosis [,]. It has demonstrated antitumor activity in cutaneous KS, with complete responses reported in approximately one-third of patients and partial responses in another third. Several studies have also reported no recurrence after one year of follow-up []. In addition, an open-label phase I-II study in HIV-negative patients reported a response rate of 47% with good tolerability []. … Intralesional vincristine has been reported as a safe and effective treatment for nodular lesions, with complete response rates of up to 76% []. Similarly, bleomycin combined with electroporation (electrochemotherapy) has demonstrated complete response rates of 65-89% []. … In one series, 63% (19/30) of patients achieved complete remission without recurrence [].
claims.locator: Revenko A, Shirron N, Shainer R, et al. (narrative review), Cancers (Basel) 2026;18(6):1008 (doi 10.3390/cancers18061008), 'Classic Kaposi Sarcoma: Current Treatment Strategies and Emerging Therapeutic Approaches', published 20 March 2026, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13024955/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **The aim is control, symptom relief and quality of life, not cure.** The preferred first-line drugs are paclitaxel and pegylated liposomal doxorubicin (PLD).
claims.locator: European Dermatology Forum, European Association of Dermato-Oncology and EORTC (Lebbé C, et al.), European Journal of Cancer 2019;114:117–127, 'Diagnosis and treatment of Kaposi's sarcoma: European consensus-based interdisciplinary guideline (EDF/EADO/EORTC)', published June 2019, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ejca.2018.12.036, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **PLD 20 mg/m² every 3 weeks:** response 76% in HIV-related KS on antiretrovirals and higher in classic KS; responses last a median of about 5 months (HIV) and 25 months (classic). Grade IV neutropenia and hand–foot syndrome each occur in about 5%.
claims.locator: European Dermatology Forum, European Association of Dermato-Oncology and EORTC (Lebbé C, et al.), European Journal of Cancer 2019;114:117–127, 'Diagnosis and treatment of Kaposi's sarcoma: European consensus-based interdisciplinary guideline (EDF/EADO/EORTC)', published June 2019, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ejca.2018.12.036, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Paclitaxel 100 mg/m² every 2 weeks** gives about 60% response in HIV-related KS. Against PLD in a randomised trial, progression-free survival was similar (17.5 vs 12.2 months) but toxicity was greater, so it is second line in HIV-related KS.
claims.locator: European Dermatology Forum, European Association of Dermato-Oncology and EORTC (Lebbé C, et al.), European Journal of Cancer 2019;114:117–127, 'Diagnosis and treatment of Kaposi's sarcoma: European consensus-based interdisciplinary guideline (EDF/EADO/EORTC)', published June 2019, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ejca.2018.12.036, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **For non-AIDS KS, the preferred paclitaxel schedule is 80 mg/m² weekly,** continuously or 3 weeks on and 1 off.
claims.locator: European Dermatology Forum, European Association of Dermato-Oncology and EORTC (Lebbé C, et al.), European Journal of Cancer 2019;114:117–127, 'Diagnosis and treatment of Kaposi's sarcoma: European consensus-based interdisciplinary guideline (EDF/EADO/EORTC)', published June 2019, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ejca.2018.12.036, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Vinblastine, oral etoposide and bleomycin are alternatives,** not first-line choices.
claims.locator: European Dermatology Forum, European Association of Dermato-Oncology and EORTC (Lebbé C, et al.), European Journal of Cancer 2019;114:117–127, 'Diagnosis and treatment of Kaposi's sarcoma: European consensus-based interdisciplinary guideline (EDF/EADO/EORTC)', published June 2019, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ejca.2018.12.036, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **PLD (S2): 20–30 mg/m² intravenously every two to three weeks.** In a randomised trial it beat bleomycin-vincristine (response 46% vs 25%). Hand-foot syndrome and mucositis limit the dose; NCCN advises an echocardiogram before starting and periodically after.
claims.source_text: Clinically, PLD achieves high response rates with a favorable safety profile and is typically administered intravenously at 20-30 mg/m2 every two to three weeks []. In a randomized trial, PLD demonstrated superior efficacy and tolerability compared with the bleomycin-vincristine combination in KS, with an overall response rate of 46% with PLD versus 25% with the combination []. … PLD is primarily associated with palmar-plantar erythrodysesthesia and mucositis as dose-limiting toxicities []. Other adverse effects include mild myelosuppression and reduced cardiotoxicity compared with conventional doxorubicin; however, current National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) guidelines recommend an echocardiogram prior to initiating treatment, followed by periodic reassessment.
claims.locator: Revenko A, Shirron N, Shainer R, et al. (narrative review), Cancers (Basel) 2026;18(6):1008 (doi 10.3390/cancers18061008), 'Classic Kaposi Sarcoma: Current Treatment Strategies and Emerging Therapeutic Approaches', published 20 March 2026, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13024955/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **S2 ranks PLD as the preferred first-line systemic therapy for classic KS, keeping taxanes for PLD resistance or intolerance;** no randomised trial compares systemic therapies head to head in classic KS.
claims.source_text: A critical limitation in CKS management is the absence of head-to-head randomized controlled trials comparing systemic therapies. Consequently, clinical consensus is largely based on retrospective analyses and data derived from HIV-associated cohorts. Within this framework, PLD remains the preferred first-line systemic therapy for CKS, due to its favorable safety profile and well-established efficacy. While taxanes are typically reserved for cases of PLD resistance or intolerance. Other chemotherapeutic agents, including vinblastine, gemcitabine, vinorelbine, etoposide, and bleomycin, may be considered second-line alternatives but are generally not recommended as first-line treatments [].
claims.locator: Revenko A, Shirron N, Shainer R, et al. (narrative review), Cancers (Basel) 2026;18(6):1008 (doi 10.3390/cancers18061008), 'Classic Kaposi Sarcoma: Current Treatment Strategies and Emerging Therapeutic Approaches', published 20 March 2026, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13024955/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Weekly paclitaxel in the largest classic-KS cohort:** complete response 15.9%, partial 63.7%, stable 13.6% (disease control over 90%). Nab-paclitaxel needs no steroid premedication and is better tolerated by older patients; neutropenia is the main dose-limiting toxicity.
claims.source_text: In the largest CKS-specific cohort to date [], weekly paclitaxel (80-100 mg) achieved complete responses in 15.9%, partial responses in 63.7%, and stable disease in 13.6% of patients, resulting in disease control in more than 90% of cases. Nab-paclitaxel, an albumin-bound formulation of paclitaxel, avoids the need for steroid premedication and is generally better tolerated in elderly patients with CKS []. … Neutropenia represents the main dose-limiting toxicity, along with fatigue and peripheral neuropathy [].
claims.locator: Revenko A, Shirron N, Shainer R, et al. (narrative review), Cancers (Basel) 2026;18(6):1008 (doi 10.3390/cancers18061008), 'Classic Kaposi Sarcoma: Current Treatment Strategies and Emerging Therapeutic Approaches', published 20 March 2026, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13024955/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Pomalidomide gave an 80% response in HIV-negative KS (phase I/II)** and is FDA-approved for KS in HIV-negative patients and in HIV-positive patients after antiretroviral failure; watch for liver and bone-marrow toxicity. Lenalidomide is less active (up to 40%).
claims.source_text: In HIV-negative KS, pomalidomide achieved a response rate of 80% in a phase I/II trial and is now FDA-approved for KS in both HIV-positive (after ART failure) and HIV-negative patients, with generally good tolerability, but potential hepatotoxicity and myelotoxicity []. Lenalidomide has shown more modest activity, with response rates ranging from none to partial response rates up to 40% of patients [].
claims.locator: Revenko A, Shirron N, Shainer R, et al. (narrative review), Cancers (Basel) 2026;18(6):1008 (doi 10.3390/cancers18061008), 'Classic Kaposi Sarcoma: Current Treatment Strategies and Emerging Therapeutic Approaches', published 20 March 2026, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13024955/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Checkpoint inhibitors are active in classic KS:** nivolumab plus ipilimumab gave 78–93% response in 18 elderly patients (grade 3–4 events 22%), and pembrolizumab 71% in classic and endemic KS. Indirect evidence suggests higher and more durable responses than antiangiogenic drugs, but they have not been compared directly.
claims.source_text: In a phase II trial of 18 elderly patients with progressive classic KS, nivolumab plus ipilimumab achieved a response rate of 78-93%. Toxicity was manageable, with grade 3-4 adverse events occurring in 22% of patients []. In a multicenter, single-arm, phase II study that included patients with classic and endemic KS, pembrolizumab achieved an overall response rate of 71%, with durable responses and an acceptable safety profile []. … Currently, no direct comparative trials have been conducted between immunotherapy and antiangiogenic agents in CKS. Indirect evidence suggests that immunotherapy may provide higher response rates and more durable remissions
claims.locator: Revenko A, Shirron N, Shainer R, et al. (narrative review), Cancers (Basel) 2026;18(6):1008 (doi 10.3390/cancers18061008), 'Classic Kaposi Sarcoma: Current Treatment Strategies and Emerging Therapeutic Approaches', published 20 March 2026, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13024955/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **S2's summary table of systemic therapy for classic KS (adopted from NCCN):** first line, pegylated liposomal doxorubicin (response 60–80%; neutropenia, nausea, asthenia); second line for refractory disease, paclitaxel (75–80%; neutropenia, alopecia, peripheral neuropathy, myelosuppression, myalgias), or nab-paclitaxel if paclitaxel is not tolerated; antiangiogenic pomalidomide (70–80%; neutropenia, hepatotoxicity, thrombosis); immunotherapy with nivolumab plus ipilimumab (87%; hepatotoxicity, GI toxicity, pneumonitis) or pembrolizumab (62–71%; pruritus, fatigue, arthralgia).
claims.source_text: [Table 1] Recommended Systemic Therapies for Classic Kaposi sarcoma *. claims.locator: Revenko A, Shirron N, Shainer R, et al. (narrative review), Cancers (Basel) 2026;18(6):1008 (doi 10.3390/cancers18061008), 'Classic Kaposi Sarcoma: Current Treatment Strategies and Emerging Therapeutic Approaches', published 20 March 2026, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13024955/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Trials under way in KS (S2 Table 2):** abemaciclib (CDK4/6 inhibitor, phase I/II), ixazomib (proteasome inhibitor, phase II), NHS-IL12 alone or with M7824 (phase I/II) and EphB4-HSA (phase II) were recruiting; a phase I study of efineptakin alfa (NT-I7, an IL-7 agonist) was terminated.
claims.source_text: [Table 2] Selected and ongoing notable clinical trials in cKS. [Table 2 row 1] Drug: Abemaciclib · Mechanism of Action: Blocks cell cycle by binding to CDK4/6, by preventing phosphorylation of RB · Study ID: NCT04941274 · Status: Recruiting · Study Design: Phase I/II study assessing the safety and efficacy of abemaciclib in participants with previously untreated or treated KS. · End Point (Primary Goal): Safety and tolerability and ORR [Table 2 row 2] Drug: efineptakin alfa (NT-I7) · Mechanism of Action: An IL-7 agonists, binds to IL-7 receptor on CD-4+ and CD-8 cells, stimulating their proliferation · Study ID: NCT04893018 · Status: Terminated · Study Design: Phase I Study of for Patients with or without Infection with HIV · End Point (Primary Goal): Adverse events [Table 2 row 3] Drug: Ixazomib · Mechanism of Action: Inhibits 20S subunit of proteosome, causing accumulation of misfolded proteins, thus causing apoptosis in malignant cells · Study ID: NCT04305691 · Status: Recruiting · Study Design: phase II trial, determine the overall response rate and safety of ixazomib in participants with Kaposi sarcoma · End Point (Primary Goal): ORR [Table 2 row 4] Drug: NHS-IL12 or in combination with M7824 · Mechanism of Action: Recombinant immunocytokine, enhances immune activation by delivering IL-12 in tumour site · Study ID: NCT04303117 · Status: Recruiting · Study Design: This is a Phase I/II study assessing the safety and efficacy of NHS-IL12 or in combination with M7824 for patients with advanced KS · End Point (Primary Goal): Safety, tolerability and activity [Table 2 row 5] Drug: EphB4-HSA · Mechanism of Action: Inhibiting EphB4-ephrin-B2 signaling pathway, crucial for tumor angiogenesis and vascular remodelling · Study ID: NCT03993106 · Status: Recruiting · Study Design: phase II trial studies toxicity and clinical response · End Point (Primary Goal): Clinical response and toxicity
claims.locator: Revenko A, Shirron N, Shainer R, et al. (narrative review), Cancers (Basel) 2026;18(6):1008 (doi 10.3390/cancers18061008), 'Classic Kaposi Sarcoma: Current Treatment Strategies and Emerging Therapeutic Approaches', published 20 March 2026, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13024955/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Low-dose interferon for classic KS is 3–5 million IU subcutaneously three times a week,** now rarely used. Sirolimus works in post-transplant KS but has shown no meaningful benefit in classic KS.
claims.source_text: In classic KS, responses have also been reported with low-dose interferon, administered at 3-5 million IU subcutaneously three times weekly []. However, this treatment is now rarely used and supporting clinical data remain limited. … However, sirolimus has not demonstrated meaningful benefit in classic KS, as its immunosuppressive effects may outweigh its antitumor activity [].
claims.locator: Revenko A, Shirron N, Shainer R, et al. claims.claim: **HIV-related KS: start antiretroviral therapy first;** most lesions regress. Add chemotherapy for poor-prognosis (T1) or rapidly progressive disease, and to prevent or treat IRIS.

claims.claim: **With antiretrovirals, liposomal anthracyclines are first line and taxanes second.** The herpesvirus (KSHV) cannot be cleared and KS can recur; if long-term cytotoxics are not tolerated, pomalidomide or lenalidomide may be discussed.

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Post-transplant KS: reduce immunosuppression to the lowest level and switch to an mTOR inhibitor such as sirolimus** while protecting the graft; add systemic therapy for extensive or life-threatening disease. Avoid interferon alfa (rejection risk).

claims.claim: **Classic/endemic KS needs systemic treatment when aggressive** (nodal or visceral disease, severe oedema, complications or rapid spread): usually liposomal anthracycline, less often weekly taxane. Low-dose interferon alfa is an option under 70 with normal cardiac function.

claims.claim: **Life-threatening disease (extensive HIV-KS, IRIS, severe post-transplant KS): review at least monthly and image at least every 3 months until stable.** Indolent classic KS can be seen every six months to a year, mainly clinically. Repeat biopsy only for atypical course or to confirm nodal or visceral spread.
